name: coding-practices
description: Applies implementation and review standards for completeness, validation, control flow, naming, comments, error handling, state, explicit options, and testing. Use before writing, modifying, refactoring, or reviewing code in any language.
---

# Coding Practices

Follow more specific repository conventions when they differ. Apply every relevant rule below.

## Completeness

Deliver complete behavior at the repository's quality bar. A release may omit features, but existing behavior must be sound. Do not leave TODOs, placeholder implementations, or temporary shortcuts. If work cannot be completed now, open an issue instead of leaving an unactionable comment.

## Assertions and Defensive Checks

Validate data at function boundaries. Use assertions for programmer errors and explicit exceptions for user or external input.

Pair checks across related paths. Validate data before writing it to a store and validate it again after reading it back. Check both what must be true and what must not be true, especially at valid-invalid boundaries.

Aim for at least two assertions or defensive checks in each behavior-bearing function. A function without checks should only wire calls together or delegate work.

## Control Flow

Use direct control flow and extract helpers before nesting becomes difficult to follow. Split compound conditions when each branch needs to be independently clear.

Consider whether an `else` should document the unhandled path. State invariants positively, such as `index < length`, rather than through negated boundary checks. Keep function bodies near 50 lines; longer functions usually contain more than one responsibility.

## Naming

Choose exact nouns and verbs that give the reader the correct mental model. Do not abbreviate names when the full term is clearer. Prefer names such as `source`, `target`, and `message_count` over `src`, `dst`, and `msg_cnt`.

Place units and qualifiers after the main noun, such as `latency_ms_max`, so related names sort together. Prefer paired names with similar length, and do not reuse one term for different meanings across subsystems.

## Comments and Documentation

Comments should explain why a choice exists so a reader can judge the tradeoff. Put a short description at the top of each test file that states the covered behavior and how the tests check it. Write comments as complete sentences; brief inline labels are acceptable.

## Error Handling

Handle every signaled error. Do not use a bare catch. Catch a broad exception only when the handler logs and re-raises, translates it into a meaningful domain error, or completely handles the failure. Trace each failure path, and make every caller deal explicitly with failures it can receive.

## Scope and State

Keep state small and local. Declare variables close to first use. Do not duplicate state that can drift from its source. Keep few variables alive at once so misuse remains easy to detect.

## Explicit Options

Spell out options at call sites when defaults affect behavior. Be explicit about encoding, timeouts, sort order, and other settings whose defaults could change or hide intent.

## Testing

The usual stack is Python backends with static HTML and JSON or YAML configuration, but repository conventions control. When adding functionality, update coupled test expectations such as tool or test counts. Run the full test suite after code changes.

name: frontend-design
description: Build or revise product-specific web interfaces with design-system discipline and rendered verification. Use for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or TypeScript frontend work including marketing pages, dashboards, forms, settings, authentication, components, empty states, and responsive UI.
---

# Frontend Design

Treat frontend design as a closed system: understand the product and its visual language before adding UI. Distinctiveness should come from product evidence, information hierarchy, and precise composition instead of generic decoration.

## Authority

Explicit user requirements and approved design specifications govern first. Existing project components and conventions govern next. Use this package's defaults only to fill gaps. Ask one focused question when those authorities conflict; never create a second visual language silently.

## 1. Detect the design context

Inspect relevant source before planning markup. Find theme and token files, typography and icon conventions, layout primitives, component libraries, nearby pages, and frontend validation scripts.

| Mode | Evidence | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Existing system | Several token and component categories are established | Reuse them |
| Partial system | Some visual conventions exist | Preserve them and fill only uncovered needs |
| Greenfield | No meaningful visual system exists | Define the smallest semantic token set and reusable primitives needed for this task |
| Ambiguous | Signals conflict | Ask which direction governs the work |

Continue only after recording the mode and the files that support it.

## 2. Select an archetype

Read [`../../standards/page-archetypes.md`](../../standards/page-archetypes.md) completely. Choose the closest archetype before implementation. A feature inside an established application normally uses the component or application-feature archetype unless it replaces an entire page.

The selection is complete when every required region or state is accounted for and genuinely inapplicable items are marked as such.

## 3. Define hierarchy and evidence

Use [`../../standards/task-brief.md`](../../standards/task-brief.md) to state the working contract:

```text
page purpose and user
primary task and primary action
optional secondary action
required content and section order
concrete product evidence
components and tokens to reuse
responsive behavior
accessibility requirements
```

Prefer a real product interface, then real data, code or terminal output, a technical or process diagram, and finally a product-specific illustration. When interface copy changes, read [`../../standards/content-standards.md`](../../standards/content-standards.md) completely before drafting it.

Move on when every section supports the primary task and the archetype's first viewport contains the required product evidence.

## 4. Establish implementation constraints

Read these files completely before changing frontend source:

- [`../../standards/frontend-standards.md`](../../standards/frontend-standards.md)
- [`../../standards/forbidden-patterns.md`](../../standards/forbidden-patterns.md)

An existing system owns component behavior and visual values. Use approved components with named variants. Treat shared design-system source and standards as protected during product UI work. If a required capability is missing, report the exact gap and ask before changing the design system or adding a one-off variant. In partial and greenfield systems, place new values in reusable semantic tokens rather than scattering raw values through feature code.

Implementation may begin once every component and visual value has an established source or one clearly defined new semantic source.

## 5. Build the smallest complete slice

Implement in reading order. Preserve semantic HTML and keyboard behavior. Keep focus visible and honor reduced-motion preferences. Cover each state the feature can enter, including disabled or selected behavior and any loading, empty, success, or error result. Keep action priority and content order intact as the viewport changes.

Motion should explain feedback or continuity. A card should mark a useful boundary or grouped interaction.

Finish this step only when the requested flow works through every applicable state and representative width.

## 6. Run repository checks

Run the actual frontend checks found in step 1. Exercise available linting and compilation, behavior tests, accessibility checks, and visual tests. Do not invent script names. Do not update visual baselines unless the task explicitly authorizes a reviewed baseline change.

Every available check must pass. For an unavailable category, record the evidence showing that the repository does not provide it.

## 7. Verify rendered output

Capture the affected interface with project browser tooling when possible. Otherwise use another available browser automation tool. Review these representative viewports:

```text
390 x 844
768 x 1024
1440 x 900
```

Inspect primary interactions and visible focus where practical. Read [`../../standards/visual-review-rubric.md`](../../standards/visual-review-rubric.md) completely, score the render, fix each critical failure and applicable violation, then capture the corrected result once.

When browser access is unavailable, apply the same rubric to source and state that rendered verification could not run. Completion requires a passing review or a concrete external blocker for every remaining failure.

## Completion report

State the archetype and context mode. Name reused or added system resources, the product evidence shown, every command and result, screenshot paths or the browser limitation, and any unresolved design-system capability or external blocker.

name: tdd
description: Test-driven development for behavior-bearing code. Use whenever TDD Guard is active, when building features or fixing bugs, or when the user requests test-first work, red-green development, or integration tests.
---

# Test-Driven Development

Work in vertical Red → Green slices. This skill defines test quality and workflow; the Pi extension and Probity enforce source writes at tool boundaries.

Read `CONTEXT.md` when present, relevant ADRs, project instructions, and nearby tests before choosing a seam or naming behavior.

## Choose a public boundary

A public boundary is where behavior can be observed without reaching into implementation details.

When an existing public seam is obvious, state it briefly and proceed. Ask the user before writing a test only when the contract is unclear or materially different seams would produce different designs, costs, or coverage.

Tests should remain valid when internals are refactored without changing behavior.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for boundary guidance.

## Write tests worth keeping

A good test describes caller-visible behavior through a public interface. Its expected value comes from an independent source such as a worked example or known literal. It fails when behavior is absent or wrong, survives internal restructuring, and makes one logical behavioral claim.

Private-method tests, internal call assertions, and project-owned collaborator mocks couple the suite to implementation. Expected results that repeat the implementation calculation or compare a value to itself are tautological. Write one test, learn from its result, and then choose the next case.

## Run one vertical slice

**Red:** Add one behavior-driving test and run the narrow relevant command. Confirm the failure comes from the expected assertion or behavior mismatch. Failures during test loading or setup do not establish a clean red. When infrastructure prevents the assertion from running, add only the placeholder needed to reach it.

**Green:** Add the minimum production behavior required by the observed failure. Run the narrow test again, followed by the broader relevant suite. Start the next behavior with a new red test.

Do not write all tests first and implementation later. Each cycle is a tracer bullet informed by the previous result.

## Refactoring

Refactoring is optional review work, not a mandatory step between every Red → Green slice. Refactor only while relevant tests are green. Do not introduce new behavior during refactoring.

## Guard interaction

Use Pi's `edit` and `write` tools for source changes so Probity can inspect pending content. Do not mutate source through shell redirection, in-place editors, patch commands, inline scripts, or other bypasses.

A guard block is evidence that the pending write lacks a valid TDD justification. Address the named problem. Do not weaken the test, alter expected behavior to match broken code, disable the guard, or search for another write path.

Only the user may disable enforcement with `/tdd off` or authorize a specific exception in the conversation.

# RepoPrompt Build

Use the user's request as the task.

Start with Git status. Locate the repository root before asking RepoPrompt to inspect anything.

Call `repoprompt_context_builder` with a precise task description and `response_type: "plan"`. Review its plan and assumptions before changing files. Call `repoprompt_workspace_context` when you need the complete selected context. Ask the user only when an unresolved choice would materially change behavior or scope.

Implement through Pi `edit` and `write`. The OrbStack repository mount is read-only, so never use RepoPrompt `apply_edits` or `file_actions`. Follow repository test-first rules for behavior changes. Run focused tests after each change, then run broader relevant checks.

Do not improvise.

Use `repoprompt_oracle_send` only for a specific question left open by Context Builder. Continue with the returned `chat_id` rather than starting an unrelated conversation.

For substantial changes, run RepoPrompt review against the final Git diff. Report changed files and commands run. Include validation results and remaining risks. Do not claim completion while required checks fail.

description: |
  Delegate work to builtin or custom subagents with single-agent, parallel,
  scripted, compatibility-chain, async, forked-context, and coordinated workflows. Use
  for advisory review, implementation handoffs, and multi-step tasks where a

# Pi Subagents

This skill is for the main parent orchestrator only. Do not inject or follow it inside spawned child subagents. The parent session owns delegation, orchestration, review fanout, and final fix-worker launches. Ordinary children should not run their own subagent workflows; the explicit exception is a delegated fanout child whose resolved builtin `tools` includes `subagent`, and that child may use `subagent` only for the fanout work the parent assigned.

Use this skill when the parent orchestrator needs one specialized child or composed orchestration. Use `workflowScript` for all execution, including one isolated child. Use `return runs.run("main", { agent, task })` for one child and `runs.all([...])` for coordinated waves: sequence, parallelism, branching, retries, gate monitors, and aggregation. Scripted workflows start asynchronously by default; pass `async:false` only for a small foreground run.

## How to use this router

Read the matching reference file before acting. Paths are relative to this `SKILL.md`; resolve them against `skills/pi-subagents/` and load them with the read tool.

| Task | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Decide whether to delegate, choose agents, compare tool versus slash commands, apply prompt techniques, or understand builtin roles | `references/prompting-and-roles.md` |
| Run one-child, scripted, async, scheduled, mission-backed, forked, watchdog, oracle, or intercom-coordinated workflows | `references/execution-controls.md` |
| List/create/update/delete/eject/disable agents or chains, edit agent files, use prompt-template integration, or expose extension RPC | `references/management-authoring-rpc.md` |
| Check safety constraints, best practices, standard workflows, or error handling | `references/constraints-and-recipes.md` |

For broad or uncertain requests, read more than one reference. For complex work, start with `references/prompting-and-roles.md` and `references/execution-controls.md`, then consult `references/constraints-and-recipes.md` before launching or reviewing child work.

## Always-on constraints

- Keep the parent as orchestrator and final decision-maker.
- Use one writer per cwd/worktree unless isolated worktrees are intentional.
- For cross-codebase work, record the target repo, explicit `cwd`, authority boundary, and expected output before launch. Do not assume the parent session cwd is the child repo.
- For parallel fanout, compare child prompts before launch. Do not send clone prompts with only issue numbers, titles, or broad file globs swapped; each child needs a lane-specific task, source seam, prior evidence, and decision that remains distinct without the item number. Launch that fanout as one async `workflowScript` with stable keys and aggregate output unless there is truly only one child.
- Prefer fresh-context review/validation fanout, then synthesize and apply fixes in the parent.
- Use async/background by default when work can proceed independently; do not poll just to wait. For adaptive gates, branch in `workflowScript`. Approval controls remain available only for already-running durable legacy chains.
- Preserve capability ceilings, including child tool restrictions and session-scoped allowed-agent restrictions.
- Escalate unresolved product, architecture, authority, release, merge, or safety decisions upward instead of letting a child decide silently.
- Treat receipts, CI, review bots, and external-run records as evidence, not authority to merge, close, comment, publish, or release.
- As a conservative orchestration policy, do not pass `turnBudget`, a hard `toolBudget`, or a tight `usageBudget` to mutation-capable workers. The default tool budget blocks read/search tools rather than mutation tools, and reported usage has no reservation model. If a worker is interrupted after a tool call starts, checkpoint after the current tool returns with changed files, build/test state, and commit or PR state.

# Approved Page Archetypes

Select one archetype before implementation. Preserve its required regions unless the task makes one genuinely inapplicable.

## Marketing product page

Use for a homepage or major product overview.

```text
Navigation → left-aligned value proposition → one primary action → concrete product evidence → proof or technical credibility → workflow → major capabilities → installation or usage example → final action
```

The first viewport shows a product screenshot, code sample, real data, or technical diagram. Keep the headline concrete and let content determine hero height.

## Product-detail landing page

Use for one feature, integration, or use case.

```text
Product context → specific problem → specific mechanism → product evidence → workflow → constraints or compatibility → proof → action
```

## Documentation page

```text
Documentation navigation → page title → short summary → prerequisites → sequential instructions → code examples → expected result → troubleshooting → related documentation
```

Optimize for scanning with stable anchors, constrained prose width, and copyable technical examples.

## Dashboard list page

```text
Page title → primary action → filters or search → optional summary or status → table or structured list → pagination or loading → empty state → error state
```

Prefer tables for comparable records. Keep the main action visible. Cards need a meaningful interaction boundary.

## Record-detail page

```text
Record identity and status → primary actions → key facts → main content → activity or related records → applicable result states
```

## Settings or form page

```text
Page title → scope explanation → grouped fields → inline help → validation → save or submit → separated destructive actions
```

Keep labels visible. A one-column form is the default unless users must compare values. Destructive controls remain distinct without competing with routine save behavior.

## Authentication page

```text
Product identity → authentication form → recovery path → required legal or policy links
```

A compact centered composition is acceptable. Keep decoration minimal and preserve keyboard operation or screen-reader support.

## Empty state

```text
State description → reason or context → one next action → optional compact detail
```

Keep the message brief and the action specific. Large illustrations and several competing actions obscure the recovery path.

## Error state

```text
Plain-language problem → useful cause or context → recovery action → optional support or diagnostic reference
```

Preserve user input and safe retry behavior where possible.

## Component or application feature

Use for a focused change inside an established interface.

```text
Purpose and surrounding context → information hierarchy → primary interaction → control states → result states → keyboard and screen-reader behavior → responsive behavior within the parent
```

Control states cover applicable behavior from this set:

```text
default | hover | focus | active | disabled
```

Result states use the same rule:

```text
loading | empty | success | error
```

Match surrounding tokens and components; one feature cannot introduce a new visual system.

# Frontend Task Brief

Complete this working brief before implementation. Keep each answer concrete and short.

| Field | Required answer |
|---|---|
| Change | User-visible result |
| Context mode | Existing system, partial system, greenfield, or ambiguous |
| Page archetype | One selection from `page-archetypes.md` |
| User and purpose | Who uses the interface and why |
| Primary task | Result the user must be able to produce |
| Primary action | Single most important action |
| Secondary action | At most one adjacent action, when needed |
| Required content | Information needed to understand the page, make a choice, or act |
| Product evidence | Product interface, real data, code sample, terminal output, technical diagram, workflow diagram, or product-specific illustration |
| Existing system | Layouts, components, named variants, and semantic tokens to reuse |
| Missing capability | Required design-system behavior that does not exist yet |
| Responsive behavior | Reading order and action priority at each target width |
| Accessibility | Applicable keyboard, screen-reader, contrast, focus, touch-target, or reduced-motion requirement |
| Acceptance checks | Repository scripts for linting, compilation, behavior, accessibility, and visual tests |

Account for applicable states in one line:

```text
default | hover | focus | active | selected | disabled | loading | empty | success | error
```

Resolve each missing design-system capability before introducing feature-specific styling. End by reviewing the final render against `visual-review-rubric.md`.

# Frontend Standards

## Operating principle

A strong interface reveals its product and follows one visual system. It stays restrained, reads clearly, and helps users act. Real screens or data should explain the product whenever possible. Code and workflows offer further evidence; product terminology anchors that evidence in context. Build hierarchy with scale and spacing, then reinforce it through weight or alignment.

## Design-system modes

| Mode | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| Existing system | Use established components, named variants, semantic tokens, the approved icon family, and current motion conventions. |
| Partial system | Preserve every established convention. Add only the semantic token or reusable primitive the task lacks, using the project's styling layer. |
| Greenfield | Define a small semantic foundation before composing a page. |

A greenfield foundation needs neutral surfaces and text, one brand accent, semantic status colors, named type and spacing roles, a small radius set, one elevation approach or none, one icon family, plus explicit focus and motion behavior. Page-local values need a reusable name and owner before use.

## Typography

Use one UI font family. Reserve monospace for source code and commands. It also fits terminal output or fixed-width data. Paths and identifiers may warrant it when their exact form matters.

Use named roles:

```text
caption
small
body
lead
subheading
section-heading
page-heading
```

A practical greenfield scale is:

```text
caption          12 / 16
small            14 / 20
body             16 / 24
lead             18 / 28
subheading       24 / 32
section-heading  32 / 40
page-heading     40-56 / 1.05-1.15
```

Write sentence-case text and let headings wrap naturally. Keep prose near 60 to 72 characters per line. Use regular body weight and 600 or 700 for headings or strong emphasis; limit the interface to three weights. Centered paragraphs should remain short enough to fit within two lines.

## Layout

Left alignment is the default. Centering fits authentication panels and compact empty, confirmation, or approved call-to-action regions.

Use named container roles such as `prose`, `content`, `page`, and `wide`. A practical greenfield spacing scale is:

```text
4  8  12  16  24  32  48  64  96
```

A section needs a clear purpose and one coherent content group. Give it a visible heading when context requires one. Consistent vertical spacing should expose the reading order. Empty space earns its place by improving readability or grouping.

## Visual tokens

Use neutral background and text scales with one brand accent. Status colors should map to success, warning, danger, or information. Application code consumes semantic tokens instead of raw literals.

Choose one approved elevation system or omit shadows. Functional boundaries must remain legible without decorative effects. Use project radius tokens; a practical greenfield set is `4px`, `8px`, and `12px`. Full pills belong to tags, status chips, avatars, toggles, or compact segmented controls. Primary controls use the normal component radius.

## Icons and motion

Use one approved icon family with fixed sizes and consistent stroke weights. An icon communicates meaning but does not replace a clear label. Designed icons replace emoji in interface controls.

Motion can explain state change, navigation, expansion, collapse, reordering, loading progress, or direct manipulation. Respect reduced-motion preferences. Motion must not delay content access.

## Controls and state

A visual region gets one primary action with at most one adjacent secondary action. Labels name both operation and object, as in `Install CLI`, `Create project`, `Invite teammate`, or `View documentation`.

A card should create a useful boundary, group related information, or act as an interactive unit. Plain layout often needs less chrome. Dividers or tables can supply the boundary; spacing can handle grouping.

Account for each state the feature can enter:

```text
default | hover | focus | active | selected | disabled | loading | empty | success | error
```

A state change must remain understandable without color alone.

## Accessibility

Use semantic elements with associated labels and logical reading order. Preserve keyboard operation and visible focus. Touch targets must remain usable, screen-reader names clear, and contrast compliant with WCAG AA. Reduced motion or script failure must not hide content or recovery actions.

## Responsive behavior

Review these viewports when tooling permits:

```text
390 x 844
768 x 1024
1440 x 900
```

Preserve reading order and action priority. Keep heading hierarchy and table usability intact. Form labels, touch targets, and required content must also survive each reflow. Adapt the composition deliberately instead of shrinking its desktop form until it fits.

# Forbidden Frontend Patterns

Each pattern below requires explicit authorization in the task, an approved design specification, or an established design-system implementation. Without authorization, use the replacement shown.

## Typography

| Pattern | Required replacement |
|---|---|
| Decorative display or multiple font personalities | Established UI family with semantic weight |
| Monospaced marketing labels | UI type role; reserve monospace for technical content |
| Italic, gradient, oversized, or manually broken headings | Semantic heading role with natural wrapping |
| Uppercase, widely tracked eyebrow labels | Sentence-case context label |
| Arbitrary font sizes | Named type roles |

## Layout

| Pattern | Required replacement |
|---|---|
| Viewport-height marketing hero | Value proposition and product evidence in content-driven height |
| Centered long-form or content-heavy layout | Readable left-aligned measure |
| Empty space used as spectacle | Spacing that clarifies grouping and reading order |
| Generic feature-card row | Structure driven by the actual content |
| Repeated cards without a useful boundary | Plain layout, list, table, or divider |
| Arbitrary container width | Named container role |
| Decorative asymmetry that harms scanning | Clear alignment system |

## Effects and imagery

| Pattern | Required replacement |
|---|---|
| Decorative gradient, glow, blurred blob, glass panel, backdrop blur, grain, noise, text shadow, or neon border | Visual and type hierarchy supported by borders and spacing |
| Several shadow systems | One approved elevation scale or none |
| Orbit, star field, floating-object collage, node network, particle field, generic AI brain, robot, or cloud art | Real interface, real data, code, workflow, or product-specific diagram |
| Abstract artwork in place of evidence | Product mechanism in the archetype's required region |

## Components and styling

| Pattern | Required replacement |
|---|---|
| Pill-shaped primary button | Standard control radius |
| Emoji used as an interface icon | Approved icon with accessible label |
| One-off variant or unapproved icon library | Normal design-system review path |

## Capability ceilings

Parent extensions may register a session-scoped, out-of-band ceiling through `pi-subagents/capability-ceiling`. Child tools and eligible canonical agent names are intersected with every active registration and inherited snapshot; `denyExtensions` removes ambient/provider extension loading while retaining package protocol runtime. `{ action: "list" }` marks non-allowlisted agents as restricted, and launch rejects them before spawn. Do not add a model-visible ceiling field or rely on unrestricted role selection for enforcement. Restricted schedules are rejected until their ceiling can be persisted safely.

## When to Use

- **Complex work orchestration**: use Fable mode as the default parent-agent loop for complex work. Complex means the task has multiple moving parts, unclear acceptance, cross-cutting code, meaningful user-visible impact, expensive or irreversible validation, broad review surface, or the user asks for orchestration. Lightweight one-off delegation can stay lightweight.
- **Advisory review**: use fresh-context `reviewer` agents for adversarial code review, or fork to `oracle` when inherited decisions and drift matter
- **Implementation handoff**: have `oracle` advise, then `worker` implement only after an approved direction
- **Recon and planning**: use `scout`, then write a plan when needed
- **Parallel exploration**: run multiple non-conflicting tasks concurrently
- **Regular skill specialists**: when discovery shows proactive skill subagent suggestions and the current work is broad enough, launch a small fresh-context fanout that asks one subagent per relevant regularly used skill to apply that skill's perspective to the task
- **Long-running work**: launch async/background runs and inspect them later. For mutation-capable work, bound the delivery slice and elapsed runtime, then request checkpoints after active tool work returns. Reserve hard turn and tool-call caps for explicitly read-only children.
- **Subagent control**: watch needs-attention signals and soft-interrupt only when a delegated run is genuinely blocked
- **Agent authoring**: create, update, or override agents and chains for a project

## Tool vs Slash Commands

Agents use the `subagent(...)` tool with `workflowScript` for execution, and `action` for management, status, and control. Humans often use the slash-command layer instead:

- `/run` — launch a single agent
- `workflowScript` — the sole public surface for sequence, parallelism, branching, retries, and aggregation
- `/subagents` — interactive admin for inspecting agents and editing model, thinking, or system prompt
- `/subagents-stop [run-id]` — stop a current-session top-level async run; opens a selector when no id is given
- `/subagents-detach [run-id]` — detach an active foreground single-subagent run without terminating its child
- `/subagent-cost` — show parent plus child token usage and cost for the session
- `/subagents-fleet` — open the live fleet inspector with per-child controls; `Ctrl+Alt+F` opens it during an active foreground turn, `↑↓`/`jk` selects children, `PgUp`/`PgDn` scrolls transcript detail, `s` steers the selected live async child, and `D` stops its top-level async run after confirmation
- `/subagents-watchdog` — inspect or configure the opt-in adversarial change watchdog (model, on/off, recommend-model, check)
- `/subagents-doctor` — diagnose setup, discovery, async paths, and intercom bridge state
- `/subagents-models [agent]` — show the live runtime-loaded builtin model mapping
- `/subagents-profiles`, `/subagents-load-profile`, `/subagents-refresh-provider-models`, `/subagents-generate-profiles`, `/subagents-check-profile` — manage model profiles and provider catalogs
- `/prompt-workflow` — run a prompt template through native workflowScript execution

Prefer the tool when you are writing agent logic. Prefer the slash commands when
you are guiding a human through an interactive flow.

Packaged prompt shortcuts are also available for repeatable workflows. Treat them as reusable orchestration recipes, not just human slash commands. When the user asks for one of these shapes, or when the workflow clearly fits, apply the same pattern directly with `subagent(...)` and other tools:
- `/parallel-review` — fresh-context reviewers with distinct review angles, then synthesis
- `/review-loop` — parent-orchestrated worker, fresh-reviewer, and fix-worker cycles until clean or capped
- `/parallel-research` — combine `researcher` and `scout` for external evidence plus local code context
- `/gather-context-and-clarify` — scout/research first, then ask the user clarifying questions with `interview`
- `/parallel-cleanup` — two fresh-context reviewers (deslop + verbosity passes) for an adversarial cleanup review of the current diff

## Applying Prompt Techniques Without Slash Commands

The prompt templates in `prompts/` encode workflows the parent agent can run on demand. If the user provides a URL, issue, PR, plan, local file, screenshot, or freeform target, treat that target as the primary scope: read or fetch it before launching children, then include it explicitly in every child task. For targets outside the parent cwd, include the exact repository, explicit `cwd`, authority boundary, and expected output path in each child task. Do not depend on the parent conversation history when the recipe calls for fresh context.

### Parallel review technique

Use this when the user wants adversarial review of a diff, plan, issue, file, or implemented work. Launch fresh-context `reviewer` agents with distinct angles generated from the actual target. Common angles are correctness/regressions, tests/validation, and simplicity/maintainability; adapt for TypeScript, UI, security, docs, or large structural changes. Reviewers should inspect files and diffs directly, return concise evidence-backed findings with file/line references, and avoid edits unless the user explicitly asks for a writer pass. The parent synthesizes fixes worth doing now, optional improvements, and feedback to ignore/defer before applying anything.

### Proactive skill-specialist technique

Use this when `{ action: "list" }` reports proactive skill subagent suggestions and the user's task would benefit from perspectives the parent regularly uses. These suggestions are conservative: a skill is recommended only when it is available and referenced repeatedly by configured agents or saved chains. Treat the list as an opt-in hint for the current task, not a command to always fan out.

Default guardrails:
- Keep the fanout small: usually one or two skill-specialist children, never more than the listed recommendations or configured cap.
- Prefer `context: "fresh"` and include only the files, diff, plan, URL, or request details each child needs. Use forked context only when private/session history is essential and appropriate to share.
- Use read-only agents for analysis/review unless implementation was explicitly requested; do not create several writers in the same worktree.
- Skip proactive skill subagents for tiny questions, direct commands, highly private requests, or when the user asks not to delegate.
- Make cost and concurrency visible by using an ordinary `subagent(...)` call rather than hidden/background automation.

Example shape:

```typescript
subagent({
  workflowScript: `
    const results = await runs.all([
      { key: "deslop", agent: "reviewer", task: "Apply the available 'deslop' skill to review the current diff for concrete cleanup findings only. Do not modify files.", skill: "deslop" },
      { key: "accessibility", agent: "reviewer", task: "Apply the available 'accessibility' skill to review the UI changes for concrete issues only. Do not modify files.", skill: "accessibility" }
    ]);
    return results.map(result => result.output);
  `,
  context: "fresh"
})
```

### Review-loop technique

Use this when the user wants implementation or current diff review to continue until reviewers stop finding fixes worth doing now. Keep the loop in the parent session: one async `worker` implements or fixes, fresh-context `reviewer` agents inspect the actual repo and diff, the parent synthesizes accepted fixes, and one async forked `worker` applies them. The parent can express the sequence up front as an async/background `workflowScript` when the workflow is known, or continue with explicit follow-up workflowScript runs after each async completion. For an initial workflow, pass `async: true` so the main chat is unblocked. Treat an async implementation worker handoff as an intermediate state, not final completion, unless the user explicitly asked for worker-only work, review-only output, or to stop after implementation. Stop when reviewers find no blockers or fixes worth doing now, remaining feedback is optional or deferred, an unapproved product/scope/architecture decision appears, or the max review-round cap is reached. Default to 3 review rounds unless the user sets a different cap. Do not loop for optional polish, and do not let children launch subagents or decide the loop outcome.

As a conservative orchestration policy, do not pass `turnBudget` or a hard `toolBudget` to an implementation worker, fix worker, reviewer with edit authority, or other mutation-capable child. The default tool budget blocks read/search tools rather than mutation tools, but count limits still do not measure delivery safety. Use a narrow task plus an outer elapsed deadline with enough margin, then request a checkpoint after the current tool returns. The checkpoint should report changed files, build/test state, remaining work, and commit or PR state. An elapsed timeout is not a mutation-safe boundary and must not be used as the checkpoint trigger.

### Parallel research technique

Use this when the question needs both external evidence and local implications. Combine `researcher` for official docs, specs, ecosystem behavior, recent changes, benchmarks, and primary sources with `scout` for repository files, patterns, constraints, tests, and likely integration points. Give each child a distinct angle: external evidence, local code context, and practical tradeoffs. Ask for source links or file ranges, confidence level, gaps, and decision implications. Do not ask these children to edit unless implementation was explicitly requested.



### Gather-context-and-clarify technique

Use this at the start of non-trivial work. Launch `scout` for local context and `researcher` only when external docs, recent sources, ecosystem context, or primary evidence would materially improve understanding. Ask children for concise findings plus remaining clarification questions. Then synthesize what is known and use `interview` to ask the unresolved questions needed for shared understanding before planning or implementing.

### Parallel cleanup technique

Use this after implementation when the user wants cleanup review or when a final pass would reduce AI-slop. Launch two fresh-context `reviewer` tasks with `output: false` and `progress: false`: one deslop pass and one verbosity pass. If the `deslop` or `verbosity-cleaner` skills are available, pass the relevant skill to that reviewer; otherwise inline the criteria. Both reviewers are review-only and should flag concrete issues with severity, file/line references, and smallest safe fixes. Phrase the constraint as “Do not modify project/source files; returning findings through the configured output artifact is allowed” when you use `output` or `outputMode: "file-only"`. The parent decides what to apply and asks before making changes unless cleanup was already authorized.

### Staged fix orchestration technique

Use this when a broad diff has known reviewer findings across several items and the user wants the parent to “orchestrate subagents like a boss.” Keep the active worktree safe with a three-stage chain:

1. A parallel read-only planning fanout, one reviewer per issue cluster. Each child inspects the real diff and returns exact files, line refs, proposed fixes, and focused validation. They must not edit.
2. One writer worker. It receives the reviewer summaries through `{previous}`, the parent’s accepted scope, stop rules, and verification contract. It is the only child allowed to edit the active worktree.
3. A parallel read-only validation fanout. Validators inspect the worker diff from fresh context with distinct angles, report pass/fail, remaining blockers, and missing verification.

Prefer `async: true`, `context: "fresh"` for reviewers/validators, `outputMode: "file-only"` for large summaries, and per-stage output names that will not collide. Add `phase` and `label` to make async status readable, and use `as` plus `{outputs.name}` when a later step needs a specific earlier result instead of the whole `{previous}` blob. Use this pattern instead of launching several writer workers into a dirty worktree. Include non-blocking suggestions in the writer prompt only when they are small, safe, and do not expand product scope; otherwise record them as deferred.

When one child returns a structured target list, use ordinary JavaScript to validate/filter it and map bounded entries into `runs.all`; do not use the removed chain fanout DSL.

  context: "fresh",

      { agent: "reviewer", phase: "Planning", label: "Deploy docs", as: "deployPlan", task: "Plan fixes for deploy docs/workflow. Inspect the current diff. Do not modify project/source files; returning findings via the configured output artifact is allowed.", output: "validation/sandbox.md", outputMode: "file-only" }
    ], concurrency: 2 }
